Two examples: FOPO's S10 dual 15.6-inch (FOPO's fit range 12.0–17.3 in, $299.99 on 2026-11-18) needs two video-capable USB-C ports, or one plus HDMI, and FOPO says it does not support base M1/M2/M3 MacBooks. FOPO's S788 16-inch triple (FOPO's range 12–18.5 in) runs through FOPO's own display driver.
standout_why: I read WorkCocoon (rank 1 in both chats) and Cevaton's 17-inch blog (rank 9 in chat 1). WorkCocoon gives no dollar prices at all. Its fit claims come from product titles ('13-17"'), and it covers USB-C Alt Mode only in general terms, never for a named product. It does not mention the base M-chip MacBook limit or that charging-only USB-C ports carry no video. Cevaton's blog gives no prices and no fit range for any product, and it does not mention drivers or DisplayLink. Graded Picks would not load (certificate error). I did not open The Office Journal, TwelveTabs, LBD Software or iTechGuides, so I can't say what they lack.
decides: For a 17-inch laptop, the first test is whether the maker's own fit range reaches 17 or 17.3 inches. Of the Mobile Pixels screens we link, both the Trio 3 Pro and the Duex Float 2 Pro are rated for 15–16-inch laptops by Mobile Pixels, so they drop out. Two FOPO models pass: the S10 dual 15.6-inch (12.0–17.3 in) and the S788 16-inch triple (12–18.5 in). Cevaton's T2 Pro passes too (13–17 in, in its title). The second test is the video path. The S10 and Cevaton's screens are driver-free but need a video-capable USB-C port for each screen, or USB-C plus HDMI on the S10. Many 17-inch Windows laptops have HDMI, so the S10 fits them without a driver. The S788 uses FOPO's UsbDisplay driver, which is the route that also works on laptops short of video ports. The Arzopa A1M ($139.99) is a freestanding 17.3-inch screen with a kickstand. It is the cheapest way to add a screen the same size as the laptop's, but it does not attach to the laptop.
